script_blocks:
In August of 2011, someone listed a single video game cartridge for sale online for one million dollars. Not a signed guitar, not a rare painting, not a car — a plastic game cartridge, the kind of thing you'd find loose in a shoebox at a garage sale, the kind most people would glance at and put right back down. The seller had bought it four years earlier for about sixteen thousand dollars. Now they wanted sixty times that, and by their own listing, they weren't taking offers.

The game was Tetris. Not the version you're picturing, though — not the one that shipped with practically every computer and console on the planet through the nineties. This was a version Sega built for its own Genesis console back in 1989, and here's what makes this one genuinely different from every other find on this channel: nobody hid this cartridge, and nobody kept it secret on purpose for decades. Sega itself tried to destroy every copy before the game ever reached a store shelf. It very nearly succeeded. Depending on which account you trust, somewhere between six and ten cartridges escaped that order. That's the entire known surviving population of a game built by one of the biggest companies in the industry.

So why would a company deliberately erase its own product days before launch? The answer has almost nothing to do with the game itself, and everything to do with a courtroom on the other side of the world while Sega's factory line was still running. In 1989, Tetris was tangled in one of the messiest ownership fights in the history of video games — a Soviet government agency, a British software house, an American arcade giant, and Nintendo, all claiming the rights to the same simple falling-blocks puzzle at the same time. Sega got caught directly in the crossfire of a war it wasn't even the main party to, and the cartridge sitting in a stranger's listing for a million dollars in 2011 is the leftover physical evidence of exactly how that war ended.

To understand how a puzzle game turns into a legal war, you have to start in Moscow in 1984, with a computer engineer named Alexey Pajitnov, working at the Soviet Academy of Sciences on a machine he wasn't technically supposed to be using for personal projects. Tetris was the result — simple, instantly addictive, and, because he'd built it on state-owned equipment inside the Soviet Union, not exactly his to sell. The rights belonged, on paper, to the Soviet government, administered through a trade agency called Elektronorgtechnica, ELORG for short.

What happened over the following five years is the part that turns a puzzle game into an actual case study in how not to license software. A Hungarian-American businessman named Robert Stein, running a company called Andromeda, flew to Moscow claiming to have secured the rights and started sublicensing the game westward before his own deal with ELORG was technically finalized. Two British publishers, Mirrorsoft and Spectrum Holobyte, ended up with home computer rights through that chain. Separately, Atari Games believed it had secured the arcade and console rights through its own negotiations. And Nintendo, hearing that a genuinely great puzzle game was about to launch its brand-new Game Boy into a licensing mess, sent a Dutch board game importer named Henk Rogers straight to Moscow to negotiate with ELORG directly, in person, face to face with Soviet trade officials.

Rogers came back with something the other parties didn't have: an actual, specific, exclusive console license, personally confirmed by ELORG. Nintendo used it to put Tetris on the Game Boy in 1989, a decision that's since been credited with helping sell tens of millions of the handheld on the strength of one simple game alone. Atari Games' console division, a company called Tengen, went ahead and released its own unlicensed Tetris cartridge for the NES anyway, apparently believing its own paperwork still held up. Nintendo sued. The case dragged through federal court, and Nintendo won — a judge ordered Tengen's unlicensed cartridges recalled and destroyed, and the ruling made it unmistakably clear that Nintendo, and only Nintendo, held the console rights ELORG had actually signed away.

It's worth sitting with just how strange Rogers's trip actually was for a moment, because it's easy to skip past as a footnote. This was 1989. The Cold War hadn't ended. A private businessman flying into Moscow to hand-negotiate a software license directly with a Soviet state trade agency, with no real precedent for how that kind of deal was even supposed to work, was about as close to uncharted territory as commercial licensing got that decade. Nintendo was betting an entire hardware launch on the outcome. The Game Boy needed a system-selling game, and Tetris — simple enough to explain in ten seconds, hard enough to keep someone playing for hours — was exactly that, if Nintendo could actually secure it cleanly. Rogers came back with the deal. Tengen's competing NES cartridge, released without that same clean paperwork, is the reason a federal court eventually got involved at all.

Sega was not a party to that lawsuit. Sega hadn't gone around Nintendo, hadn't released anything without a license, and by most accounts genuinely believed its own arrangement to put Tetris on the Genesis was legitimate and separate from the NES fight entirely. It didn't matter. As the legal picture around console rights snapped into focus in early 1989 — Nintendo, and only Nintendo — Sega's own Mega Drive cartridge, already built, already boxed, already sitting on a factory line ready to ship, became collateral damage in a war being fought entirely between other companies.

What happened next depends on which account of Sega's internal decision-making you believe, because the company never gave a detailed public explanation at the time, and there's no court filing that spells out Sega's side of it the way the Tengen ruling spells out Atari's. The most consistent version, repeated across multiple retro-gaming outlets that have dug into this story over the years, is that Sega halted production of its own accord rather than risk the same legal fate Tengen had just been handed — and then went further, pulling back and destroying the units that had already come off the line. Production stopped, in one account, right as it was starting. The recall wasn't limited to unsold retail stock sitting in warehouses; it reportedly reached back into cartridges that had already been manufactured and boxed for a launch that was, by then, only weeks away.

I want to be upfront about something here: nobody, including the outlets that have covered this story for over a decade, claims to know the exact internal mechanics of how thorough that destruction actually was, or precisely how many cartridges slipped past it before the order came down. What's consistently reported, across every serious source I could find, is the outcome — a fully manufactured, essentially finished Sega Genesis game, made by a major console manufacturer, that was pulled and destroyed days before it would have simply been sold in stores like any other cartridge that year.

The stakes for Sega weren't abstract, either. This wasn't a small budget cartridge or a side project — it was a mainline release for the Genesis, Sega's flagship console at the time, going up directly against Nintendo in the middle of the most competitive console war the industry had seen yet. A finished, working version of one of the most popular puzzle games on the planet would have been a genuine selling point for the platform. Pulling it, days before launch, wasn't a minor inventory adjustment. It was Sega walking away from a real piece of its own lineup rather than risk becoming the next company a federal judge ordered to destroy its own stock.

Here's the number that actually matters for everything that happens next: how many copies got out before Sega's own recall caught up with them. And the honest answer is that nobody agrees, precisely, because there was never an official count published by anyone. One retro-gaming outlet that's covered the story since 2009 puts the figure at around six. Other outlets, along with the record later kept by Guinness World Records itself, describe it more cautiously as fewer than ten. Nobody's claiming a hundred. Nobody's claiming two. It's a genuinely small, genuinely uncertain number sitting somewhere in the low single or low double digits, and I'd trust any source that states it with more confidence than that a little less for it.

What isn't in dispute is what happened to the value of those surviving cartridges once collectors realized what they actually were. A finished, fully licensed-looking Sega product that the company itself tried to erase is about as close to a manufactured legend as this hobby produces, and genuine surviving copies have been reported selling for over sixteen thousand dollars — not as a one-time fluke, but as a documented, repeated price point across more than one sale. For a single cartridge with a plastic shell and a few chips inside it, sitting in the same category, price-wise, as a used car.

One of those surviving copies came with something the others didn't: a signature. At some point after acquiring the cartridge, its owner had it personally signed by Alexey Pajitnov himself — the same Moscow engineer whose 1984 side project had, five years and one messy international lawsuit later, ended up costing Sega an entire finished product line. A signed, documented, one-of-a-kind survivor of a cartridge its own manufacturer had tried to wipe out of existence. That's the specific copy that turns up next, in the summer of 2011, on an ordinary online auction listing with an asking price that made international headlines.

The listing appeared on eBay on August the 2nd, 2011, posted by a user going by the name shinsnk, based in the small Catalan town of Hostalric in Spain. The item: an original Japanese Sega Mega Drive Tetris cartridge, autographed by Alexey Pajitnov, described by the seller as essentially unique. The asking price: one million American dollars, listed as a straight buy-it-now, not an opening bid for others to haggle down.

According to reporting from the time, the seller had bought the cartridge roughly four years earlier for eleven thousand euros — a little under sixteen thousand dollars at the exchange rate then — and had since turned down offers as high as twenty thousand dollars from other collectors before deciding to list it publicly at a price nobody could quietly negotiate around. Gaming outlets picked the story up almost immediately, most of them landing somewhere between genuine fascination and open disbelief that anyone would actually pay seven figures for a single game cartridge, however rare. Guinness World Records eventually recognized the listing outright, naming it the most valuable Tetris video game on record — a title that, notably, describes the asking price of the listing rather than a confirmed final sale amount.

And that's the honest, slightly unsatisfying place where this particular thread of the story runs out. Guinness's own record states the listing was eventually marked sold. It does not state, anywhere I could verify, what the buyer actually paid for it. No contemporary report I found names a buyer, confirms a closing price, or documents where the cartridge physically ended up afterward. It's entirely possible it sold for the full million. It's also entirely possible — maybe even more likely, given how these listings tend to actually resolve — that a private, undisclosed offer well under that number is what actually closed the deal, the way high six-figure asking prices on rare collectibles often do settle in practice. I'm not going to manufacture a tidy ending here that the record itself doesn't support.

Coverage from the time captures the tone well. Some outlets treated it as a straightforward collector's-market headline; others couldn't quite hide their disbelief that a single cartridge, however rare, was being priced somewhere in the range of a house. What almost every writeup agreed on, though, was the basic shape of the story underneath the number: a game Sega itself tried to erase, surfacing seven years after that failed recall, priced at a figure meant to reflect not what it would cost to replace — nothing could replace it — but what it might take to convince someone who already owned one of the last surviving copies to actually let it go.

So here's what this story actually is, once you strip away the headline number. A game that was never supposed to exist commercially in the first place — finished, packaged, and then deliberately destroyed by its own manufacturer over a legal fight it lost no part in — became, purely because of how few copies survived that destruction, one of the single most valuable pieces of plastic in the entire video game hobby. Not because it's a particularly good version of Tetris. By every account, it plays roughly like Tetris always plays. Its value has nothing to do with the game underneath the label and everything to do with the fact that Sega itself tried to make sure you'd never be able to buy one.

What we can say with real confidence: somewhere between six and ten cartridges are believed to exist. Ordinary surviving copies, unsigned, have documented sales north of sixteen thousand dollars. And one specific copy, signed by Tetris's own creator, was listed for a million dollars in August of 2011 and was, per Guinness World Records, eventually marked sold — with the actual closing price never publicly confirmed anywhere I could find. That's the complete, honest version. Not a clean seven-figure payday with a name and a date attached to it, but a genuinely strange piece of corporate history that a small handful of collectors happen to be sitting on right now, mostly out of public view.

If there's a takeaway here that isn't just "check your old game collection" — though, for what it's worth, it's genuinely worth doing that too — it's this: sometimes the rarest thing in a market isn't the object somebody tried hardest to protect. It's the one somebody tried hardest to erase, and simply didn't quite manage to finish the job.

There's a pattern worth noticing here, one this channel keeps circling back to in different forms: the things that end up worth the most are rarely the ones somebody deliberately set aside because they already knew what they had. More often, value shows up afterward, attached to whatever happened to survive an accident, a mistake, or — in this particular case — a company's own attempt to make sure nothing survived at all. Sega wasn't trying to create a collector's item in 1989. It was trying to cut its losses quietly and move on. The fact that a handful of cartridges slipped through anyway is the entire reason this story exists thirty-five years later.

_источники.policy: Every core claim tagged VERIFIED / SINGLE SOURCE / DISPUTED / LEGEND. Disputed items are flagged in narration, not asserted.
do_not_claim: Точное число сохранившихся картриджей — источники расходятся ('шесть или около того' у Sega-16, 'меньше десяти' у Guinness World Records и других изданий). Сценарий прямо называет это неопределённостью, а не выбирает одну цифру.

Финальная цена продажи листинга 2011 года — Guinness World Records подтверждает только пометку 'sold', но не называет итоговую сумму. Ни один из проверенных источников (Engadget, Tom's Guide, Game Informer, Old School Gamer Magazine, Rolling Stone, Ubergizmo) не приводит подтверждённую цену закрытия сделки. Сценарий явно проговаривает, что закрытие сделки за полный $1,000,000 не подтверждено.

youtube.description_intro: In 1989, Sega finished, boxed, and then deliberately destroyed its own Tetris cartridge for the Genesis — collateral damage in a legal war fought between Nintendo, Atari, and a Soviet trade agency. Fewer than ten copies are believed to have survived. In 2011, one of them was listed on eBay for one million dollars.
chapters: A Million Dollars for a Cartridge
youtube.description_notes: Sources disagree on the exact number of surviving Sega Mega Drive Tetris cartridges (estimates range from about six to under ten). Guinness World Records confirms the 2011 eBay listing was marked sold but does not state the final closing price — no source checked for this video confirms the cartridge actually sold for the full $1,000,000 asking price.
